title: Hello, my name is Ani
title_target: សួស្ដី ខ្ញុំឈ្មោះ អានី — sua-sdey, khnyom chhmuah 'aa-nii
goal: Greet people, say your name, ask how someone is, and choose the right word for "yes" — because in Khmer that word depends on whether the speaker is a man or a woman.
bekal: greet people with សួស្ដី and reply
say your name with ខ្ញុំឈ្មោះ …
choose between បាទ and ចាស without hesitating
ask and answer how someone is with សុខសប្បាយទេ?
say what country you're from with មកពី …

dialogs.title: កិច្ចសន្ទនា — In front of a house in Phnom Penh
dialogs.intro: Ani has just arrived in Phnom Penh to work for a year. Sokha, the next-door neighbor, greets her at the gate. Notice one thing from the very first line: Sokha ends his sentences with បាទ, while Ani ends hers with ចាស — and both mean "yes".

lines.speaker: សុខា:
lines.text: [សួស្ដី|sua-sdey]! [ខ្ញុំ|khnyom] [ឈ្មោះ|chhmuah] [សុខា|so-khaa] [បាទ|baat]។

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [សួស្ដី|sua-sdey]! [ខ្ញុំ|khnyom] [ឈ្មោះ|chhmuah] [អានី|'aa-nii] [ចាស|chaah]។

lines.speaker: សុខា:
lines.text: [អានី|'aa-nii] [មកពី|mòòk-pii] [ប្រទេស|pra-teh] [ណា|naa] [បាទ|baat]?
lines.id: Which country are you from, Ani?

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [ខ្ញុំ|khnyom] [មកពី|mòòk-pii] [ប្រទេស|pra-teh] [ឥណ្ឌូនេស៊ី|'en-do-né-sii] [ចាស|chaah]។ [ពី|pii] [ក្រុង|krong] [ហ្សាការតា|jaa-kaa-taa]។
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia. From the city of Jakarta.
lines.literal: I — come-from — country — indonesia — yes(f). from — city — jakarta.

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [សុខសប្បាយ|sok-sap-baay] [ចាស|chaah]។ [អរគុណ|'aa-kun]។ [បង|baang] [សុខា|so-khaa] [វិញ|weñ]?
lines.id: Fine. Thank you. And you, Bong Sokha?
lines.literal: healthy-happy — yes(f). thank-you. older-sibling — sokha — in-return?

lines.speaker: សុខា:
lines.text: [ខ្ញុំ|khnyom] [ក៏|kaa] [សុខសប្បាយ|sok-sap-baay] [ដែរ|dae] [បាទ|baat]។ [អានី|'aa-nii] [ចេះ|chéh] [ភាសា|phie-saa] [ខ្មែរ|khmae] [ទេ|té]?
lines.id: I'm fine too. Do you speak Khmer, Ani?
lines.literal: I — also — healthy-happy — too — yes(m). ani — know — language — khmer — (question)?

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [បន្តិច|ban-tech] [ចាស|chaah]។ [ខ្ញុំ|khnyom] [កំពុង|kam-pung] [រៀន|rien]។

lines.speaker: សុខា:
lines.text: [ល្អ|l'aa] [ណាស់|nah]! [នេះ|nih] [ជា|chiè] [ប្អូនស្រី|p'oun-srey] [ខ្ញុំ|khnyom] [បាទ|baat], [ឈ្មោះ|chhmuah] [ស្រីមុំ|srey-mom]។
lines.id: Very good! This is my younger sister, her name is Sreymom.
lines.literal: good — very! this — is — younger-sister — I — yes(m), name — sreymom.

lines.speaker: ស្រីមុំ:
lines.text: [សួស្ដី|sua-sdey] [អានី|'aa-nii]។ [រីករាយ|riik-riey] [ដែល|dael] [បាន|baan] [ជួប|chuèp] [ចាស|chaah]។
lines.id: Hello, Ani. Nice to meet you.
lines.literal: hello — ani. glad — that — got-to — meet — yes(f).

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [ខ្ញុំ|khnyom] [ក៏|kaa] [រីករាយ|riik-riey] [ដែរ|dae] [ចាស|chaah]។ [បង|baang] [នៅ|neuw] [ទីនេះ|tii-nih] [ទេ|té]?
lines.id: Nice to meet you too. Do you live here?
lines.literal: I — also — glad — too — yes(f). older-sibling — live — here — (question)?

lines.speaker: សុខា:
lines.text: [បាទ|baat], [នៅ|neuw] [ទីនេះ|tii-nih]។ [អញ្ជើញ|'añ-cheuñ] [ចូល|choul] [ផឹក|pheuk] [តែ|tae]។
lines.id: Yes, I live here. Please come in and have some tea.
lines.literal: yes(m), live — here. please — enter — drink — tea.

grammars.title: ⚠️ បាទ versus ចាស — "yes" depends on the SPEAKER's gender
body: English uses one word, "yes", for everyone. Khmer doesn't. The word you choose depends on **who is speaking**, not on who you are speaking to — and that choice never changes for the rest of your life.

head: Speaker
Word
Say it
Used for
rows: "yes", and a politeness word at the end of a sentence
"yes", and a politeness word at the end of a sentence

after: These two words do double duty. As an answer, they mean "yes". Attached to the end of any sentence, they become a politeness marker — like adding "sir" or "ma'am" in English. ខ្ញុំមិនយល់ means "I don't understand"; ខ្ញុំមិនយល់ទេ បាទ sounds much more polite.

⚠️ The most common mistake is treating them like "yeah" and "yep", which anyone can use. A man who says ចាស sounds as if he is imitating a woman; a woman who says បាទ sounds like a soldier. Nobody is offended — but everyone will smile, and you won't know why.

grammars.title: ខ្ញុំឈ្មោះ … — introducing yourself without "is"
body: ឈ្មោះ (*chhmuah*) means "name", but in a sentence it works as a **verb**: "to be named". So ខ្ញុំឈ្មោះអានី is literally "I am-named Ani" — there is no "is" anywhere, and Khmer doesn't need one.

head: English
Khmer
Say it
rows: ខ្ញុំឈ្មោះ អានី
អ្នកឈ្មោះអ្វី?
គាត់ឈ្មោះ សុខា
ខ្ញុំជាជនជាតិឥណ្ឌូនេស៊ី

after: ⚠️ Look at the last row: that's where ជា (*chiè*) appears, and **that** is the Khmer word for "is". It is used only to link two nouns (I = an Indonesian). It is **never** used before an adjective. "I'm happy" is not ខ្ញុំជាសប្បាយ but ខ្ញុំសប្បាយ — because in Khmer adjectives are verbs. Unit 14 covers this in full.

grammars.title: ទេ — one small word with two jobs
body: ទេ (*té*) appears twice in this dialogue doing two completely different jobs, and beginners often get confused. The rule is actually simple: **the position is the same; the job depends on whether មិន stands before the verb.**

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: ចេះភាសាខ្មែរទេ?
ខ្ញុំមិនចេះទេ

after: ⚠️ Look at the second row. To say "yes" to a ចេះ…ទេ? question, Cambodians **repeat the verb** rather than saying "yes". English does something similar — "Do you speak Khmer?" "I do." — so you just carry the habit over.

Khmer negation has two fences: មិន before the verb, ទេ at the end of the sentence. Forgetting ទេ is the number-one mistake in the first year, because English needs only one "not". Unit 4 covers it in full.

blocks.text: These five sentences are enough for a whole first introduction. Memorize them as one block, then swap in your own details. The last line uses the male politeness word; women simply change បាទ to ចាស.

Khmer
Say it

ខ្ញុំមកពីប្រទេសឥណ្ឌូនេស៊ី
ខ្ញុំកំពុងរៀនភាសាខ្មែរ
រីករាយដែលបានជួប បាទ

blocks.title: Three things that make you sound natural right away
items: **Press your palms together in front of your chest when you greet someone.** This is called សំពះ (*sam-peah*). The higher your hands, the more respect: chest height for people your age, mouth height for elders or superiors, forehead height for monks. Saying សួស្ដី without the សំពះ feels half-done.
**Use the other person's name, not a pronoun.** Cambodians say "Would Ani like some tea?" rather than "Would you like some tea?". Using a name sounds warm; អ្នក ("you") sounds distant.
**Add វិញ (*weñ*) to turn a question back.** After saying how you are, just say the other person's name followed by វិញ — សុខា វិញ? It's the same as "and you?" and saves a whole sentence.
